strengths: Addresses a clear and practical limitation of prior tool-creation methods (reliance on LLM internal knowledge) by grounding tool synthesis in structured external reference materials (textbooks), which is a sensible and useful idea.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three distinct domains (causality, physics, chemistry) and four different LLM backbones (Llama-3.1-70B, Gemini-1.5-Pro, GPT-4, GPT-4o), with consistent improvements over general-reasoning baselines, RAG baselines, general tool-creation methods (Creator), and domain-specific reasoning methods (Physics Reasoner, StructChem, ChemAgent).

Well-designed ablation study isolating the contributions of code-form tools vs. raw text (PoT+Hierarchical RAG) and hierarchical selection vs. similarity-based retrieval (REFTOOL sim), providing evidence that both components matter.
Human evaluation of tool quality (faithfulness, correctness, usefulness) and of consistency between LLM and human tool/chapter selection adds credibility beyond automated metrics alone.
Cost analysis showing REFTOOL is substantially cheaper and faster than comparable iterative/domain-specific methods (e.g., ChemAgent, Physics Reasoner) is a meaningful practical contribution.
Reasonable robustness checks: alternate tool-creation LLM (Gemini), reasoning model (o1-mini), and an additional unseen dataset (SciBench-fund) to test generalization/reusability of created tools.
Clear presentation with illustrative figures, case studies, and detailed prompts/appendix for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The performance gains, while consistent, are often modest and inconsistent across models/domains (e.g., in Chemistry, ChemAgent nearly matches or is close to REFTOOL for some models; in Physics, GPT-4 with PoT+REFTOOL barely beats PoT alone: 49.1 vs 45.6, and REFTOOL sometimes underperforms RAG or Creator on individual backbones, e.g., Llama-3.1-70B in Physics RAG 44.7 vs REFTOOL 53.5 is better but GPT-4 causality PoT+REFTOOL 38.7 is worse than ReAct+RAG 48.0), raising questions about the robustness/generality of the 11.3% average improvement claim, which appears sensitive to which baselines/models are aggregated.

The method fundamentally depends on the existence of a single well-matched, well-structured reference book per domain; the paper does not explore scenarios with multiple/overlapping/lower-quality references, conflicting reference sources, or domains lacking a clean hierarchical textbook, limiting the generality of the claimed framework beyond curated benchmark domains.

Reliance on GPT-4o (or Gemini) for tool creation contradicts the framing that REFTOOL overcomes 'the model's internal knowledge scope' — the tool-creation LLM must still correctly parse and interpret the reference material, so the approach does not fully escape the underlying model's comprehension limits (as acknowledged in the Limitations section, but not deeply investigated quantitatively, e.g., by measuring correlation between tool-creation model's domain competence and quality of resulting tools).

Benchmark scale is relatively small (114–269 questions per domain, and even smaller sub-datasets for chemistry, e.g., 118 total across three sub-datasets), which combined with the fairly small differences between methods raises concerns about statistical significance; no significance testing or variance/multiple-run analysis is reported.

The tool-creation process requires manually curating an appropriate, licensed textbook per domain and converting to LaTeX with preserved hierarchical structure — this human/engineering effort before running REFTOOL is nontrivial and somewhat downplays the 'human-free' framing claimed in the introduction.

The hierarchical tool selection mechanism (chapter then tool selection) is relatively simple (LLM prompted to pick from table of contents), and its comparison against a single alternative (embedding similarity retrieval) is somewhat narrow; other stronger baselines for hierarchical or agentic retrieval (e.g., iterative refinement, cross-encoder reranking) are not explored.

Novelty is somewhat incremental: the core techniques (LLM-based code tool synthesis, execution-based validation/refinement, hierarchical retrieval) are each individually well-established in prior tool-creation and RAG literature; the main contribution is combining them with reference grounding, which, while useful, is a natural extension rather than a fundamentally new technique.

The chemistry-domain human evaluation shows lower tool quality (89% example correctness) attributed to the LLM misunderstanding nuanced domain concepts, which is a red flag for scalability of the approach to more advanced or less textbook-friendly domains, but this issue is not explored further or mitigated.
